entry: Branch of mathematics concerned with how functions can best be approximated by simpler functions, and with the errors this introduces. What counts as best or simpler depends on the application. A closely related topic is the approximation of functions by generalized [[Fourier series]], which sum terms based on orthogonal polynomials. A key problem is approximating a function in a computer mathematical library using only operations the machine performs, such as addition and multiplication, so that the result is as close as possible to the actual function. This is typically done with [[Polynomial]] or rational approximations, made more accurate by using a higher-degree polynomial or a narrower domain. Modern libraries often divide the domain into many tiny segments and use a low-degree polynomial on each. The optimal polynomial minimizes the worst-case error; by the equioscillation theorem, an Nth-degree polynomial whose error oscillates between +ε and −ε N+2 times is optimal.

Fruit, or the tree that bears it, of several species in the genus *Prunus*, usually *Prunus armeniaca*. World production in 2023 was 3.7 million [[Tonne|tonnes]], led by [[Turkey]] with 20% of the total. *Prunus armeniaca* was domesticated in ancient times in [[Central Asia]] and [[China]], and cultivation spread across Eurasia and to [[North Africa]] and Japan. The fruit is eaten fresh and dried, and used in [[Cake|cakes]], tarts and jam as well as in savory dishes. The tree grows up to 8 m (26 ft) tall and bears white or pinkish flowers before its leaves appear in spring. Apricot trees need 300 to 900 chilling units and tolerate winter temperatures as low as −30 °C (−22 °F) if healthy. The kernels contain amygdalin, which can release [[Cyanide|cyanide]] if eaten in excess.

Either of the two extreme points in the orbit of a celestial body about its primary body. The nearest point is the periapsis and the farthest the apoapsis, and the line joining them is the line of apsides. For orbits around [[Earth]] the terms are perigee and apogee; for orbits around the [[Sun]], perihelion and aphelion. The same terms apply to the orbits of planets, [[Comet|comets]] and [[Asteroid|asteroids]] in the [[Solar System]].

Region in southern Italy (pop., 2026: 3,865,277), with its capital at [[Bari]]. Bordered by the Adriatic Sea to the east, it covers 19,540.90 sq km (7,544.78 sq mi). It was ruled in turn by the Romans, Byzantines, Normans, Aragonese and Spanish, became part of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, and was annexed to the [[Kingdom of Italy|unified Kingdom of Italy]] after the Expedition of the Thousand.

Persianate, Sunni Muslim Turkoman tribal confederation (1378–1508). Founded in the Diyarbakir region by Qara Yuluk Uthman Beg, it ruled parts of present-day [[Turkey|eastern Turkey]] and, in its last decades, [[Armenia]], Azerbaijan, much of [[Iran]], Iraq and Oman. Its empire reached its zenith under Uzun Hasan (r. 1453–1478), who built a centralized sultanate with Persianate administration and codified laws. The ruling family belonged to the Bayandur clan of the Oghuz Turks. The confederation fought constant wars with the rival [[Qara Qoyunlu]], and in 1402 it allied with [[Timur]] against the Ottomans at the Battle of Ankara. Shah Ismail I of the Safavids took its core territories in 1501, and its rule ended by 1508.

Highly corrosive mixture of [[Nitric acid|nitric acid]] and [[Hydrochloric acid|hydrochloric acid]], optimally in a 1:3 molar ratio. The name is [[Latin]] for 'royal water'. Alchemists named it for its ability to dissolve noble metals such as [[Gold|gold]] and platinum while leaving many other metals unaffected. Freshly prepared, it is colorless but turns yellow, orange or red within seconds as nitrosyl chloride and nitrogen dioxide form. It is used primarily to produce chloroauric acid, the electrolyte in the Wohlwill process for refining the highest purity (99.999%) gold, and in etching and analytical procedures.

Controlled cultivation of aquatic organisms such as fish, [[Crustacean|crustaceans]], mollusks, algae and aquatic plants. Also called aquafarming, it contrasts with commercial fishing, which harvests wild fish. It involves freshwater, brackish and saltwater populations kept under controlled or semi-natural conditions, and it is also used to restore marine and freshwater [[Ecosystem|ecosystems]]. Onshore facilities such as tanks, ponds and aquaponics depend on human control of water quality, feed and temperature, while inshore and offshore systems expose stock to more natural conditions, including ocean currents. Reported global output was over 120 million [[Tonne|tonnes]] valued at US$274 billion in 2019; by 2022 it had risen to 130.9 million tonnes, valued at USD 312.8 billion, although the reliability of reported figures is uncertain. Some forms cause nutrient pollution and disease transfer to wild populations.

Vivarium of any size with at least one transparent side, in which aquatic plants or animals are kept and displayed. The term, coined by English naturalist Philip Henry Gosse, combines the [[Latin]] *aqua* ('water') with the suffix *-arium*. In 1850 chemist Robert Warington explained that plants in a container of water could give off enough [[Oxygen|oxygen]] to support animals, so long as their numbers stayed small. The craze was launched in England in 1853, when Gosse created and stocked the first public aquarium, at the London Zoo. Large public aquariums may keep [[Dolphin|dolphins]], [[Shark|sharks]], [[Penguin|penguins]] and [[Whale|whales]] alongside fish and other species. Home aquaria are usually constructed of [[Glass|glass]] or acrylic. Flat-walled aquaria are called fish tanks, while round-walled ones are fish bowls.

Watercourse built to carry water from a source to a distribution point far away. The term, from [[Latin]] *aqua* ('water') and *ductus* ('led'), now covers any system of pipes, ditches, canals and tunnels used for this purpose, and also a bridge carrying an artificial watercourse. Aqueducts were devised in [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]], the Near East, the Indian subcontinent and pre-Columbian Mexico and Peru, and are most associated with the Romans. Roman-style aqueducts appeared as early as the 7th century BC, when the [[Assyria|Assyrians]] built an 80 km long aqueduct to carry water to their capital at [[Nineveh]]. Underground systems called falaj in [[Oman]] and qanāts in Persia drew water through well-like vertical shafts linked by gently sloping tunnels, delivering it by gravity in dry climates. Modern aqueducts may use [[Pipeline|pipelines]]; the 444-mile California Aqueduct, operating since 1973, carries water from the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta to southern [[California]].

Underground layer of permeable rock or loose material, such as gravel, sand or silt, that holds water. Groundwater from aquifers can be sustainably harvested through [[Well|wells]] for drinking water, agriculture and industry. Overdrafting, which extracts water beyond what the aquifer can replenish, can lower the water table and cause land subsidence and salinization. In 2013, large offshore aquifers containing low-salinity water were found under the continental shelves of Australia, China, North America and South Africa.

Neotropical genus of macaws, with eight extant species and at least two extinct ones. Erected by French naturalist Bernard Germain de Lacépède in 1799, the genus name comes from the Tupi word *ará*, an [[Onomatopoeia|onomatopoeia]] of the macaw's call. Ara macaws are large parrots with long tails, long narrow wings and vividly colored plumage, and all have a bare facial patch around the eyes. Males and females look alike. The genus ranges from [[Mexico]] to [[Argentina]], centered on the Amazon Basin and the Panama–Colombia border region. The scarlet macaw was designated the type species. Many Ara are popular in the pet trade, and bird smuggling threatens several species. The extinct Cuban macaw was last confirmed in 1864, when one was shot.

Series of wars from the 7th to 11th centuries between the successive Islamic caliphates and the [[Byzantine Empire]]. After the Byzantine defeat at the Battle of the Yarmuk, [[Early Muslim conquests|Muslim armies]] took most Byzantine territory in the Levant, Egypt and North Africa within decades. Syria was captured in 639 and Egypt in 642. Umayyad forces twice placed [[Constantinople]] under siege, in 674 to 678 and 717 to 718, without taking it, and the border then stabilized at the Taurus Mountains. Abbasid vassals conquered [[Crete]] in 827 and took [[Sicily]] between 831 and 878. From c. 920 to 976 the Byzantines pushed Arab forces back in Anatolia, and Crete was reconquered in 961. The [[Fatimid Caliphate]] later replaced the Abbasids as the main Arab power in the Levant. Byzantine defenses used [[Greek fire]], a naphtha-based incendiary weapon, which proved devastating in naval engagements.

Conflict between Israel and surrounding Arab states, rooted in the [[Israeli–Palestinian conflict]]. Zionists viewed Palestine as the Jewish ancestral homeland and sought to establish a Jewish state or homeland there through colonization, while Arabs generally opposed [[Zionism|Zionism]] and regarded Palestine as Arab Palestinian land. The [[League of Nations]] gave Britain the Mandate for [[Mandatory Palestine]] in 1920, following agreements including the [[Balfour Declaration|Balfour Declaration]]. Intercommunal violence became civil war in 1947, after the United Nations adopted the Partition Plan for Palestine, and an international war began when Israel was declared on May 14, 1948. The 1948 war ended with the 1949 Armistice Agreements, which established the Green Line. Further wars followed in 1956, 1967, 1973 and 1982. Peace treaties were later signed with Egypt and Jordan, and the Abraham Accords of 2020 further calmed relations. Historians differ on the causes: some Israeli historians, such as Anita Shapira, locate them in Arab rejection of Jewish self-determination, while Palestinian narratives emphasize the displacement of Palestinians in 1948.

Regional organization of Arab states, founded in [[Cairo]] on March 22, 1945. It began with seven members, Egypt, Iraq, Transjordan, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Syria and North Yemen, and now has 22, including three non-Arab countries: [[Comoros]], [[Djibouti]] and [[Somalia]]. Its stated aim is to draw closer relations between member states, coordinate their collaboration and safeguard their independence and sovereignty. Each member has one vote on the Council, and decisions bind only the states that voted for them. The League has achieved a relatively low level of cooperation throughout its history, though it has sought to settle interstate disputes and limit conflicts, such as the 1958 Lebanon crisis. In March 2015 it announced a Joint Arab Force to counter extremism and other threats.

Series of pro-democracy protests, uprisings and armed rebellions across much of the Arab world in the early 2010s. It began in [[Tunisia]] after the self-immolation of Mohamed Bouazizi and spread to Libya, Egypt, Yemen, Syria and Bahrain. Zine El Abidine Ben Ali of Tunisia, [[Muammar Gaddafi|Muammar Gaddafi]] of Libya and Hosni Mubarak of Egypt were deposed in 2011, and [[Ali Abdullah Saleh]] of Yemen in 2012. The early wave faded by late 2012, as many demonstrations met violent responses, and major conflicts followed in Syria, Iraq, Libya and Yemen. Some refer to the period that followed as the Arab Winter. A new wave of protests from 2018 led to the overthrow of presidents Omar al-Bashir of Sudan and Abdelaziz Bouteflika of Algeria in 2019. In December 2024 a rebel offensive led to the [[Fall of the Assad regime|fall of the Assad regime]] in Syria.

Geocultural region of West Asia and North Africa, where Arabic is the lingua franca. It is usually defined as the 19 states in which Arabs form at least a plurality of the population. At its widest it comprises the 22 members of the [[Arab League]], which also includes the non-Arab [[Comoros]], [[Djibouti]] and [[Somalia]]. The region stretches from the Atlantic Ocean to the Arabian Sea and from the Mediterranean Sea to the Indian Ocean. Its eastern part is the Mashriq and its western part the Maghreb. According to the World Bank, it had a population of 456 million and a gross domestic product of $2.85 trillion as of 2021. Other ethnic groups include Berbers, Kurds, Somalis and Nubians. The Arab League was formed in 1945 to pursue political unification, a project known as pan-Arabism.

Vast desert wilderness in West Asia, occupying almost the entire [[Arabian Peninsula]]. At 2,330,000 sq km (900,000 sq mi), it is the fourth largest desert in the world and the largest in Asia. Its southern end is Ar-Rub' al-Khali (the Empty Quarter), the largest continuous body of sand in the world. It is an extension of the [[Sahara]] Desert. Most of the area receives around 100 mm (3.9 in) of rain a year, although some places receive as little as 50 mm, and temperatures swing between intense heat and seasonal night-time freezes. Gazelles, oryx, sand cats and spiny-tailed lizards survive here. Species such as the striped hyena and [[Honey badger|honey badger]] have died out through hunting, habitat destruction and overgrazing, while the Arabian sand [[Gazelle|gazelle]] has been reintroduced and is protected at reserves. Most of the desert lies in [[Saudi Arabia]].

Peninsula in West Asia, and the world's largest, with an area of 3,237,500 sq km (1.25 million sq mi). Nine countries lie on it: Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, [[Saudi Arabia]], the United Arab Emirates and Yemen, along with the southern halves of Iraq and Jordan. It is bounded by the [[Red Sea]] to the west and the [[Persian Gulf]] to the northeast, and most of it is covered by the Arabian Desert. The peninsula formed between 56 and 23 million years ago as the Red Sea Rift opened between the African and Arabian plates. In the 7th century AD it was politically and religiously united by the Prophet [[Muhammad]]. Since the 20th century, discoveries of oil and natural gas have made it central to global geopolitics.

Sea of the northern Indian Ocean, lying between the [[Arabian Peninsula]] and the Indian subcontinent. It has an area of 3,862,000 sq km (1,491,000 sq mi) and a maximum depth of 5,395 meters (17,700 feet). The [[Gulf of Aden]] links it to the [[Red Sea]] through the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, and the Gulf of Oman connects it to the [[Persian Gulf]]. Trade was historically restricted by the [[Monsoon|monsoon]] winds and their currents. Its straits linked the Mediterranean with India, Southeast Asia and East Asia through trade networks established in the 3rd millennium BC. The sea is highly productive, but overfishing, pollution and warming have put many of its species at risk. The largest river flowing into it is the Indus, and its largest islands include [[Socotra]], Masirah and Astola.

Horse breed with historic roots in West Asia, and one of the oldest modern breeds. Its refined, wedge-shaped head and dished profile are distinctive, and most have naturally high tail carriage. The breed developed in a desert climate and was prized by nomadic [[Bedouin]] people, who often brought horses into the family tent. Selective breeding produced a horse that is good-natured, quick to learn and willing to please, with the alertness needed for raiding and war. Arabians dominate endurance riding and compete in many other equestrian fields. Foundation sires such as the Byerly Turk, Darley Arabian and Godolphin Arabian influenced the [[Thoroughbred]] and many light horse breeds, and Arabian bloodlines are now found in almost every modern riding horse breed.

Abjad, or consonantal alphabet, of the [[Arabic]] language, with 28 letters. It is written from right to left in a cursive style, and most letters take up to four forms according to their position in a word: initial, medial, final or isolated. Dots above or below the central part of a letter distinguish letters of the same basic shape. Vowels are optionally notated with diacritics, so the script is considered an impure abjad. The lām-alif ligature is the only mandatory one.

Prose and poetry written in the Arabic language. The Arabic word for literature, *adab*, derives from a sense of etiquette and implies politeness, culture and enrichment. Literature was transmitted orally until it began to be written down in the 7th century. Pre-Islamic poetry recorded tribal life, honor and satire, while its prose consisted mainly of parables, speeches and stories. The [[Quran|Quran]] had the greatest lasting effect on Arabic literature, standardizing the language and marking the start of Islamic literature, and the literature flourished during the [[Islamic Golden Age]]. Notable later figures include [[Abu Nuwas]], and the Nobel laureate [[Naguib Mahfouz]], a pioneer of the Arabic novel.

Music of the Arab world, based on the maqam system, which has long exchanged influences with neighboring musical traditions. Each country and region has its own folk, classical and modern styles, in many linguistic varieties. Pre-Islamic Arabia was an early center of musical theory and instrument development, and Hejaz was known for preferring musicians from Yemen. The theorists [[Al-Kindi]] and [[Al-Farabi]] shaped early Arabic music theory; Al-Farabi identified twelve tones on the Arabic scale, and his tone system is still in use. In 1252 Safi al-Din developed a notation in which rhythms were shown geometrically. By the 11th century, Islamic Iberia had become a center for making [[Musical instrument|instruments]] that spread into France and Europe. The English words [[Lute|lute]], rebec and naker derive from Arabic oud, rabab and naqareh.

Writing system used for Arabic and several other languages of Asia and Africa. It was first used for Arabic texts, including the [[Quran]], and spread with Islam to languages such as Persian, [[Urdu]], [[Pashto]], Uyghur, Kurdish, Malay, Indonesian and Somali. It is the second most widely used alphabetic writing system in the world, after the [[Latin script]]. Written from right to left in a cursive style, it has no capital letters, and most letters take different shapes depending on their position in a word. Most letters transcribe consonants, so many Arabic-script alphabets are abjads. The script descends from the [[Aramaic]] alphabet through the Nabataean script, whose cursive form gradually became the Arabic alphabet. It is the basis of Arabic calligraphy.

Small plant of the mustard family (Brassicaceae), widely used as a model organism in plant biology. Known as thale cress or mouse-ear cress, it is native to Eurasia and Africa and is generally considered a weed along roads and in disturbed land. It is an annual with a short life cycle, and it can complete its lifecycle in six weeks. It was the first plant genome to be sequenced, in 2000, and its genome is around 135 megabase pairs. The plant is widely used in research on [[Genetics|genetics]], [[Evolution|evolution]] and development, and has helped reveal how [[Flower|flower]] development and light sensing work. Its direct agricultural significance is small.
